title: Implement a proper Liveness probe
description: Use a liveness probe when restarting the container can recover an unhealthy application. Check local process health rather than shared downstream dependencies to avoid restart storms during an outage. Tune timeouts and failure thresholds under realistic load; failed liveness probes restart the container according to its restart policy, not the entire pod.

documentation.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

title: Implement a proper Startup probe
description: Protect slow-starting containers with a startup probe. Liveness and readiness probes do not run until it succeeds. Set failureThreshold and periodSeconds to cover measured worst-case startup time, and test cold starts; exhausting the startup failure threshold triggers container restart according to its restart policy.

documentation.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

title: Implement a proper Readiness probe
applicability: Applies to availability-sensitive services receiving traffic through Kubernetes Services or other readiness-aware routing.
description: Use readiness probes to indicate whether the application can serve traffic. A failed readiness probe normally removes the pod from ready Service endpoints without restarting its containers. Test dependency failures and recovery without making every replica unready for an optional dependency; account for endpoint propagation, existing connections, and Services that publish not-ready addresses.

documentation.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

title: Implement graceful termination and use preStop hooks when needed
applicability: Applies to availability-sensitive services or workers that must drain requests or checkpoint work during planned termination.
description: Handle termination signals, stop accepting new work, and drain in-flight requests or checkpoint work within terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Add a preStop hook only when needed and include its execution time in the grace period. Hooks and graceful shutdown are not guaranteed during node loss, force deletion, or abrupt process failure; test rolling updates and node drains.

title: Run more than one replica for your Deployment
applicability: Applies to availability-sensitive services whose design permits concurrent replicas; singleton workloads require a separately tested recovery design.
description: Run multiple ready replicas for services that require availability during pod failure or maintenance. Size the replica count and autoscaler minimum for the availability target and remaining capacity after a failure. Spread replicas across nodes and, where available, zones; extra replicas on one node are not sufficient.

title: Apply consistent Kubernetes labels and Azure resource tags
description: Apply recommended Kubernetes application labels and ownership/environment metadata for selectors, policy, operations, and cost allocation. Azure resource tags and Kubernetes labels are separate mechanisms and are not automatically synchronized. Keep secrets and personal data out of both.
detail: Define technical, business and security metadata, including owner, environment, cost center and lifecycle. Apply Azure tags through supported AKS cluster and node pool APIs and review propagation and replacement behavior before updates; do not directly retag AKS-managed infrastructure to bypass those APIs. Define deliberate mappings to Kubernetes labels and validate selectors before changing labels used by controllers or policies.

documentation.title: Use Azure tags in Azure Kubernetes Service
Azure tags and Kubernetes labels in AKS

title: Implement autoscaling of your applications (Horizontal pod autoscaler, KEDA)
description: Use HPA for resource, custom, or external metrics, or the managed KEDA add-on for event-driven scaling. Configure resource requests for utilization-based targets, minimum/maximum replicas, stabilization, and metric failure behavior. Load-test startup latency and downstream capacity; coordinate pod scaling with node capacity and quotas. Do not configure independent HPA and KEDA controllers for the same workload.

title: Use namespaces with explicit access and isolation controls
description: Use dedicated namespaces rather than the default namespace for managed workloads. Apply scoped RBAC, network policies, resource quotas, and admission controls to enforce boundaries. Namespaces alone do not provide network isolation or a strong security boundary against hostile tenants; use separate clusters when the threat model requires them.
detail: Name namespaces for application and environment ownership, reserve system namespaces for platform components, and verify that access, policy enforcement and quota behavior match the intended boundary. This control implements namespace protections after the separate tenant-isolation architecture decision.

title: Specify the security context of your pod/container
description: For Linux workloads, run as non-root, disallow privilege escalation, drop all capabilities and add back only justified exceptions, use RuntimeDefault seccomp, and make the root filesystem read-only where compatible. Avoid privileged containers, host namespaces, and hostPath mounts. Apply equivalent OS-specific controls for Windows rather than assuming Linux settings apply.
detail: Use dedicated least-privilege service accounts and set automountServiceAccountToken: false when Kubernetes API credentials are unnecessary. This does not replace the explicit projected token used by Microsoft Entra Workload ID. Provide bounded writable volumes where the application requires them and document reviewed exceptions.

documentation.title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

title: Ensure your manifests respect good practices
description: Render Helm or Kustomize manifests in CI, validate their schemas and supported API versions against the target AKS version, and check security, requests, probes, and deployment policies before promotion. Use server-side dry runs where safe and enforce critical requirements with admission policy rather than relying only on developer linting.
detail: Test rendered output against a representative target cluster to catch admission, permissions and scheduling errors. A formatter improves readability but is not evidence that APIs are supported or that the deployment is safe.

title: Conduct Dockerfile scanning to ensure Docker Image Security Best Practices
description: Define and lint a container build baseline: trusted maintained base images, non-root execution, multi-stage builds, minimal runtime contents, and no embedded credentials. Use build-time secret mounts instead of copying secrets into layers; deleting them in a later layer does not remove them from image history.

documentation.title: AKS container image management best practices

title: Scan built container images in CI before promotion
description: Scan the final image digest, including OS and application dependencies, before promotion and retain the result with the release. Integrate scanning into CI; registry or runtime scanning alone is not a synchronous build gate and cannot establish that an image is vulnerability-free.

documentation.title: Container security in the software supply chain

title: Enforce risk-based vulnerability gates for image releases
description: Gate image promotion using documented vulnerability severity, exploitability, exposure, and remediation deadlines. Record time-limited exceptions with owners and compensating controls.
detail: Do not automatically allow a critical vulnerability merely because no vendor fix exists. Require explicit risk acceptance, consider replacing or removing the vulnerable component, and rescan retained and deployed image digests as new advisories appear.

title: Compliance enforcement of Docker Image Builds
description: Evaluate image configuration and rendered deployment manifests against a documented security baseline before release, and enforce critical runtime settings through admission policy.
detail: Check non-root execution, privilege escalation, capabilities, host access, and approved image sources. An exposed port alone does not establish a compliance violation, and Azure Policy admission checks do not replace Dockerfile or build-time scanning.

title: Assess application readiness before containerization
description: Assess runtime and operating-system support, external dependencies, state, licensing, health endpoints, and shutdown behavior before moving an application into containers. Select currently supported migration or build tooling for the application stack; automated repackaging does not establish production readiness or remove the need for testing.

title: Apply the right deployment type to your application
description: Choose Deployment for replaceable services, StatefulSet for workloads requiring stable identity and storage, and Job or CronJob for finite or scheduled work. Configure rolling update surge/unavailable settings, readiness, rollout deadlines, and rollback procedures to match the workload and available capacity.

title: Don't use naked pods
description: Manage production pods with a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet, Job, or other appropriate controller. Standalone pods are not recreated on another node after node loss.
detail: Choose the controller according to lifecycle, identity, and storage requirements; a controller recreating a pod does not by itself recover data or guarantee service availability.

title: Control the usage of imagePullPolicy
description: Set imagePullPolicy deliberately and deploy immutable digests rather than mutable latest tags. Always resolves the image reference on each start but can reuse cached layers; IfNotPresent can run a locally cached image. Test registry outages and new-node image pulls; digest pinning improves reproducibility but does not remove registry availability requirements.

title: Use version-controlled infrastructure as code for Azure resources
description: Provision AKS and its dependencies with reviewed, version-controlled Bicep, ARM, or Terraform. Secure state and deployment identities, pin supported providers and modules, detect drift, and test repeatable environment recreation. Keep credentials out of templates and repositories.

documentation.title: Create a Kubernetes cluster with Azure Kubernetes Service using Terraform

title: Use canary or blue/green deployments
applicability: Applies when application-release risk and availability targets require progressive traffic shifting or parallel application versions.
description: Use canary or blue/green application releases where the risk justifies additional capacity and routing complexity. Define health and business-metric gates, progressive traffic shifts, rollback, and backward-compatible database changes. These strategies reduce release risk but do not guarantee availability during cluster upgrades.

title: Evaluate Dapr when its building blocks fit the application
applicability: Applies when Dapr is installed or an assessed application requirement justifies its building blocks; Dapr adoption is not a readiness requirement.
description: Consider Dapr for service invocation, pub/sub, state, or other supported building blocks when it reduces application complexity. Evaluate sidecar resources, component authentication, mTLS, supported versions, operations, and failure modes; adopting Dapr is optional and does not ensure uptime during cluster upgrades.

title: Design retries, timeouts, and idempotency for dependency failures
description: Set bounded request timeouts, retry budgets with exponential backoff and jitter, and circuit breakers where appropriate. Make retried operations idempotent and support graceful degradation. Test dependency throttling and outages so retries and autoscaling do not amplify failure.
